title: Taking Down Old Dams Is Helping Fish Return to Northeastern Rivers
summary:
Across the northeastern United States, old dams are coming out of streams and rivers, and fish called river herring are coming back.

A dam is a wall that blocks a river to hold back water. Dams can store water for farms and homes or make electricity. But they can also stop fish from swimming upstream to lay their eggs. Some fish, like alewives, spend part of their lives in the ocean and part in rivers.

Beginning in the 1600s, colonists in the East built many dams to power mills. By the mid-1800s, more than 65,000 mills lined eastern creeks. Scientists have calculated that over four centuries, New England's dams have cost its ecosystems nearly 20 billion pounds of alewives.

Now that is changing. Since 1912, more than 2,300 dams have been removed from US waterways, most of them in the last 25 years. Big projects in the West, such as the Klamath River in California and Oregon, get the most attention. But most removals happen in eastern states. In 2024, Pennsylvania alone removed 27 old dams.

Nathan Furey, a fish biologist at the University of New Hampshire, says that for the first time in history, barriers are being removed faster than new ones are built. Still, at least 35,000 dams block fish runs in the Northeast.

The results can be big. In 2025, about six million river herring returned to Maine's Penobscot River, 12 years after two dams there came down. That was double the number from two years earlier.

On New Hampshire's Bellamy River, where two old dams were removed, Furey's team puts tiny tags, about the size of a grain of rice, in alewives to count how many make it upstream.

Scientists say small streams matter too. "A cold-water tributary just a quarter-mile long could be really important," says Joshua Royte of the Nature Conservancy.
why_it_matters: Removing old dams can bring back fish that were blocked for centuries, showing that damaged rivers and ecosystems can recover.

background_read: Dams are walls built across rivers to store water, control floods or power machines and generators.
Fish such as river herring live part of their lives in the ocean and swim up rivers to lay eggs, so a dam can cut them off from the places they need.
In the Northeast, many small dams were built long ago to power mills that are no longer used.
Removing old dams lets rivers flow freely again, so fish can return.
